review.review: The initiating defect was preparation arbitration, not simply excessive waiting. Decisions 1203–1204 staged an unknown-potion test beside magical fire and began moving to a remote potion stash. At decision 1205 (log line 3548), required-loot priority sent the Mage back to the test square instead of advancing that stash. Decision 1206 then reported an incomplete stash (line 3551); recovery disabled further potion-supply preparation. By decision 1403 (lines 4093–4095), the observed upgrade remained unreachable behind fire, and fallback play began. The final accepted transition at decision 2946 (line 8664) reduced HP from 6 to 0 during a targeted zap; this alone does not identify the killer. A selector-only reconstruction of the short preparation episode matched the played actions and reasons at decisions 1203–1205. With the correction, the first difference is decision 1205: the existing stash controller advances instead of restarting staging. This reconstruction is not recorded runtime memory. The new deterministic regression fails on the played policy and passes on the candidate; the full suite passes 1,589 tests with four skips. The correction preserves hazard checks, unknown potion identities, drop receipts, and mandatory upgrade collection. It establishes continued preparation, not successful potion testing, fire removal, reward collection, or survival.
review.learnings: When required loot depends on potion preparation already in progress, let the existing stash workflow advance before selecting another test approach. Keep potion identities unknown until publicly established, verify every drop and pickup, and retain the upgrade obligation until collection is observed.
